items.prompt: State the name of the molecule that forms the two layers in the basic structure of a cell surface membrane.
items.canonical_answer: Phospholipid. The phospholipids form a bilayer, which is the basic structure of the membrane.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for phospholipid or phospholipid bilayer. Accept phospholipids. The feature asked for is the molecule that makes the two layers of the structure.
Do not credit protein, cholesterol or lipid on its own, because they are not the molecule that forms the bilayer.

objective_titles: describe the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure, including the components phospholipids, cholesterol, glycolipids, proteins and glycoproteins

items.prompt: Describe how phospholipid molecules arrange themselves in water to form the bilayer of a cell surface membrane.
items.canonical_answer: The heads are polar and hydrophilic, so they face outwards towards the water on both sides of the membrane. The fatty acid tails are non-polar and hydrophobic, so they face inwards, away from the water, and this forms two layers with the tails in the middle.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: the hydrophilic heads face outwards towards the water (1); the hydrophobic tails face inwards, away from the water (1); this gives two layers with a hydrophobic core in the middle (1). Maximum 2.
The mechanism is the reason: the heads face the water because they are polar, and the tails face away because they are hydrophobic. A statement of the arrangement with no reason earns 1 mark at most.

items.prompt: A learner says that the head of a phospholipid molecule is polar because of the glycerol. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to confuse the glycerol with the phosphate group. In fact the head is polar because of the phosphate group, which carries a charge, and the glycerol only joins the head to the two fatty acid tails. The test is to ask which part of the molecule carries the charge: it is the phosphate group.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the glycerol is given the job of making the head polar (1); the correct idea, that the phosphate group carries the charge and glycerol is a link between the head and the tails, or the test of which part carries the charge (1).
The card is a discrimination between two parts of one molecule, not a repeat of the description of a phospholipid.

items.prompt: A learner says that a red blood cell is surrounded by a double membrane because its membrane is a bilayer. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of two layers with two membranes. In fact a red blood cell is bounded by one membrane, which is made of two layers of phospholipid. A double membrane is an envelope of two separate membranes, as around a nucleus or a mitochondrion. The test is to ask how many membranes bound the cell and how many layers of phospholipid make the membrane: one membrane and two layers.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that two layers of phospholipid are taken to be two membranes (1); the correct idea, that the cell surface membrane is one membrane made of two layers, whereas a double membrane is the two-membrane envelope of an organelle, or the test of counting membranes and layers (1).
The card is a discrimination between a bilayer and a double membrane, not a repeat of the structure of the bilayer.

items.prompt:
The table is our description of two parts, P and R, labelled on a diagram of a cell surface membrane.

| Part | What the diagram shows |
|---|---|
| P | a small molecule lying among the fatty acid tails, in both layers |
| R | a protein on the outer surface that carries a branched chain of carbohydrate |

Describe what the diagram shows about P and R by naming each part and stating one role of each. [2]
items.canonical_answer: P is cholesterol, which regulates the fluidity of the membrane. R is a glycoprotein, which has a carbohydrate chain that takes part in cell recognition or in signalling.
marking_guidance: 2 marks, 1 for each part: P named as cholesterol with a role such as regulating fluidity or stability (1); R named as a glycoprotein with a role such as recognition or signalling, for example as an antigen or a receptor (1).

The values read from the table mean the parts must be identified from their features: among the tails shows cholesterol, a carbohydrate chain on a protein shows a glycoprotein. A role with no name earns no mark.

items.prompt: Describe two roles of the cell surface membrane.
items.canonical_answer: It is the boundary of the cell, separating the cytoplasm from the surroundings. It is partially permeable, so it controls which substances enter and leave the cell. It also carries receptors for signal molecules and antigens that identify the cell.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from four points, one for each role described: the boundary that separates the cytoplasm from the surroundings; control of what enters and leaves because it is partially permeable; receptors that detect signals from other cells; antigens that identify the cell. Maximum 2.
Each role is a function of the membrane. A role named with no description, such as a barrier, needs what is separated or controlled to earn the mark.

items.prompt: Describe how the cell surface membrane controls which substances enter and leave a cell.
items.canonical_answer: The hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer resists the passage of ions and polar molecules, but small non-polar molecules such as oxygen can dissolve in it and pass through. Channel proteins and carrier proteins let specific ions and molecules cross, because each binds or fits only the substance it moves.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: the hydrophobic core of the bilayer resists ions and polar molecules (1); small non-polar molecules pass through the bilayer (1); channel proteins or carrier proteins move specific substances across (1). Maximum 2.
The mechanism is how each part causes the control, not a statement that the membrane is partially permeable, which is the result and earns no mark on its own.

items.prompt:
The table gives our own invented values for how fast four substances cross a phospholipid bilayer that has no proteins in it.

| Substance | Relative rate of crossing the bilayer (arbitrary units) |
|---|---|
| oxygen | 100 |
| carbon dioxide | 90 |
| glucose | 1 |
| sodium ions | 0.1 |

Describe the pattern in the table and state what it means about the bilayer. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Oxygen and carbon dioxide, which are small non-polar molecules, cross at rates of 100 and 90 arbitrary units, while glucose and sodium ions, which are polar or charged, cross at only 1 and 0.1 arbitrary units. This means the hydrophobic core of the bilayer is a barrier to polar molecules and ions.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the pattern read from the data, with values, that the non-polar substances cross much faster than the polar or charged ones (1); the meaning, that the bilayer is partially permeable because its hydrophobic core resists polar molecules and ions (1).

The table shows a difference of about 100 times between oxygen and glucose, so a pattern with no values quoted earns 1 mark at most, and the meaning must refer to the core, not just to the membrane being a barrier.

items.prompt: State the name of the protein in a cell surface membrane that has a water-filled pore through which ions can pass.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for channel protein. Accept ion channel or protein channel. The feature that identifies it is the water-filled pore.
Do not credit carrier protein, which changes shape instead of forming a pore, or receptor.

items.prompt: Describe how a carrier protein moves a molecule across a cell surface membrane.
items.canonical_answer: The carrier protein binds the specific molecule on one side of the membrane. This causes the protein to change shape, and then it releases the molecule on the other side of the membrane.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: the specific molecule binds to the carrier protein on one side (1); the carrier protein changes shape (1); the molecule is released on the other side (1). Maximum 2.

The sequence matters because the change of shape is caused by the binding and leads to the release. Accept energy from ATP for movement against a concentration gradient as an extra point, with the cap kept at 2.

items.prompt: A learner says that cholesterol is the part of the membrane that faces the water on both sides and so keeps the membrane waterproof. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of cholesterol with the phospholipid heads. In fact the heads are polar and face the water, and cholesterol lies among the fatty acid tails, where it regulates the fluidity of the membrane. The test is to ask which part faces the water and which part sits among the tails.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that cholesterol is given the job of the phospholipid heads, which face the water (1); the correct idea, that cholesterol sits among the fatty acid tails and regulates fluidity, or the test of which part faces water and which sits among the tails (1).
The card is a discrimination between two parts of the membrane, not a repeat of the role of cholesterol.

items.prompt: Describe, in order, how a hormone released by a gland cell produces a response in a target cell.
items.canonical_answer: First, the gland cell releases the hormone, which is carried in the blood to the target cells. Then the hormone binds to a cell surface receptor on a target cell, because its shape is complementary to the binding site of the receptor. Finally, the binding triggers a specific response inside the target cell.
marking_guidance: 3 marks from four points in the correct order: the gland cell releases the hormone (1); the hormone is carried in the blood to the target cells (1); it binds to a complementary receptor on the cell surface membrane of the target cell (1); the binding triggers a specific response in the target cell (1). Maximum 3.
The sequence is the point: a step described out of order, or the response described before the binding, earns no mark for that step. The end result is the response of the target cell.

items.prompt: Describe how a hormone can reach many cells but cause a response in some of them and not in others.
items.canonical_answer: The hormone binds only to cells that have a receptor with a binding site complementary to it, because the shape of the receptor matches that hormone. Cells without this receptor do not bind the hormone, so no response is triggered in them.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: only cells with the matching receptor bind the hormone (1); the binding site is complementary in shape to the hormone (1); cells without the receptor do not respond because the hormone does not bind (1). Maximum 2.
The mechanism is how the receptor causes the selection of cells, not a statement that the response is specific, which is the result.

items.prompt: A learner says that in cell signalling the signal is the gland cell, and that it works like a nerve impulse along a reflex arc. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to name the signalling cell instead of the signal molecule and to confuse the process with a nerve impulse. In fact the signal is the chemical released by the cell, and it binds to a receptor on a target cell and changes what that cell does. The test is to ask whether the signal is a molecule binding to a receptor or an electrical impulse along a neurone: in cell signalling it is the molecule.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the cell or a nerve impulse is taken to be the signal (1); the correct idea, that the signal is the molecule that binds to a receptor on the target cell, or the test of molecule binding to a receptor versus an electrical impulse (1).
The card is a discrimination between a signal molecule and an impulse, not a repeat of the stages of cell signalling.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which statement describes a cell surface membrane?
A  Two separate membranes, each made of a single layer of phospholipid.
B  One membrane made of two layers of phospholipid.
C  One membrane made of a single layer of phospholipid with protein on both sides.
D  Two separate membranes, each made of two layers of protein.

2. Which part of a phospholipid molecule is polar because it carries a charge?
A  the glycerol
B  the fatty acid tail
C  the phosphate group
D  the chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms

3. Where in a cell surface membrane is cholesterol found, and what does it regulate?
A  between the fatty acid tails, the fluidity of the membrane
B  facing the water on both sides, the passage of ions
C  on the outer surface only, cell recognition
D  spanning the bilayer, the speed of active transport

4. What is a glycoprotein?
A  a lipid with a carbohydrate chain attached
B  a carbohydrate with a protein chain attached
C  a protein that spans the whole bilayer
D  a protein with a carbohydrate chain attached

5. Which part of a cell surface membrane has a water-filled pore through which ions can pass?
A  a carrier protein
B  a channel protein
C  a cell surface receptor
D  a glycolipid

6. What can bind to the binding site of a cell surface receptor?
A  any molecule that is small enough to fit into the membrane
B  any molecule that is polar
C  a molecule with a complementary shape
D  a molecule that has a carbohydrate chain

7. Oxygen crosses a phospholipid bilayer much faster than sodium ions do. Which statement explains this?
A  Oxygen is polar, so it is attracted to the phosphate groups of the heads.
B  Sodium ions are too large to fit between the heads.
C  Sodium ions are attracted to the fatty acid tails.
D  Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it dissolves in the hydrophobic core.

8. A cell is treated with a chemical that blocks all of its carrier proteins. Which movement is most directly stopped?
A  uptake of glucose against its concentration gradient
B  diffusion of oxygen into the cell
C  diffusion of carbon dioxide out of the cell
D  movement of the phospholipids sideways within a layer

9. Which sequence describes cell signalling?
A  a receptor on the signalling cell releases a molecule, then a response occurs in the blood
B  a signalling cell releases a molecule, the molecule binds to a receptor on a target cell, then the target cell responds
C  a target cell releases a molecule, the molecule binds to a receptor on a signalling cell, then the signalling cell responds
D  a molecule enters the target cell, then the cell surface receptor is made, then the target cell responds

10. A hormone reaches two neighbouring cells in a tissue. One cell responds and the other does not. Which statement is the best explanation?
A  The cell that does not respond has no cell surface membrane.
B  The hormone cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer of the second cell.
C  The cell that does not respond has no receptor with a binding site complementary to the hormone.
D  The cell that does not respond has no phospholipids in its membrane.

11. What is the signal in cell signalling?
A  the molecule released by the signalling cell
B  the signalling cell
C  an electrical impulse along a neurone
D  the receptor on the target cell

12. Which molecule on the outer surface of a red blood cell is most likely to act as an antigen?
A  a phospholipid head
B  a molecule of cholesterol
C  a fatty acid tail
D  a glycoprotein
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 C, 3 A, 4 D, 5 B, 6 C, 7 D, 8 A, 9 B, 10 C, 11 A, 12 D.
1. A cell surface membrane is one membrane made of two layers of phospholipid (B). A and D describe a double membrane, the envelope of an organelle, which is the register error of calling the bilayer a double membrane; C counts a single layer instead of two.
2. The phosphate group carries the charge (C). A is the error of explaining the polar head by the glycerol, which only links the head to the tails; B and D are the non-polar tails.
3. Cholesterol lies between the fatty acid tails and regulates fluidity (A). B is the error of giving cholesterol the job of the phospholipid heads; C and D give it the roles of glycoproteins and carrier proteins.
4. A glycoprotein is a protein with a carbohydrate chain attached (D). A describes a glycolipid; B reverses the molecules; C describes where some proteins lie, not what a glycoprotein is.
5. A channel protein has a water-filled pore (B). A is a carrier protein, a near-neighbour term that changes shape instead of forming a pore; C is a receptor, which binds a signal molecule; D is a lipid with a carbohydrate chain.
6. The binding site is complementary in shape to one specific signal molecule (C). A and B treat size or polarity as enough, but shape decides; D confuses the receptor with the carbohydrate chains of a glycoprotein.
7. Oxygen is small and non-polar so it dissolves in the hydrophobic core, whereas charged sodium ions are not attracted to it (D). A calls oxygen polar; B blames size alone, when charge is the main barrier; C reverses the attraction.
8. Carrier proteins carry out active transport, which moves glucose against its gradient (A). B and C happen through the bilayer without carrier proteins; D is sideways movement of the phospholipids, which does not depend on carrier proteins.
9. The signalling cell releases the molecule, it binds to the receptor on the target cell, then the target cell responds (B). A and C put the receptor or the response on the wrong cell; D has the molecule enter the cell and the receptor made after binding, which reverses the cause and effect.
10. The cell that does not respond lacks a receptor complementary to the hormone (C). A and D deny that the cell has a membrane or phospholipids, which every cell has; B is wrong because a hormone binds to a receptor on the outside and does not need to cross the bilayer.
11. The signal is the molecule that is released (A). B is the error of naming the signalling cell instead of the molecule; C is the error of treating cell signalling as a nerve impulse; D is the receptor, which detects the signal.
12. A glycoprotein, a protein with a carbohydrate chain on the outer surface, can act as an antigen (D). A, B and C are parts of the lipid bilayer with no projecting carbohydrate chain to identify the cell.
marking_guidance: 12 marks, 1 for each question. The key is given first, with the reason the correct option is right and the error each distractor comes from.

About half the questions test recall (1 to 6, 11) and half apply the ideas to a situation or a described sequence (7 to 10, 12). The distractors are built from the register errors first: the glycerol, the double membrane, cholesterol at the heads, and the signal taken as a cell or an impulse.

items.prompt:
These are our own invented results for a hormone, H. Three types of cell from the same tissue were each exposed to hormone H, and the table records what was found on each type and how it responded.

| Cell type | Receptor for hormone H on cell surface membrane | Receptor for a different hormone, J, on cell surface membrane | Response to hormone H |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | present | absent | glucose released from the cell |
| Q | absent | absent | no response |
| R | absent | present | no response |

(a) State the name of the molecule at the cell surface of cell P that hormone H binds to, and state where in the cell this molecule is found. [2]
(b) Describe, in order, how hormone H leaves the gland cell that makes it and causes the response in cell P. [2]
(c) Explain why cell Q does not respond to hormone H, although hormone H reaches it. [2]
(d) Cell R responds when hormone J is added. Suggest why hormone H does not cause a response in cell R. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A receptor (a protein or glycoprotein); in the cell surface membrane, on its outer surface.
(b) The hormone is released by the gland cell and carried in the blood to the target cells; it binds to the receptor on cell P, which triggers the response inside the cell, the release of glucose.
(c) Cell Q has no receptor for hormone H, so the hormone has nothing to bind to, and without binding the response is not triggered.
(d) Cell R carries a receptor for hormone J, whose binding site is complementary in shape to hormone J and not to hormone H, so hormone H cannot bind to it and no response is triggered.
marking_guidance: Marks and points: (a) 1 mark for receptor, 1 mark for the cell surface membrane (outer surface); (b) 2 marks from three points: released by the gland cell and carried in the blood, binds to the receptor on cell P, triggers the response inside the cell; (c) 2 marks from three points: no receptor for hormone H, so no binding, so no response.

(d) 2 marks from three points: cell R has a receptor for hormone J, its binding site is complementary to J and not to H, so H does not bind. Parts (a) and (b) credit AO A (4 marks); parts (c) and (d) credit AO B (4 marks). The reason must use the cells in the table, not a general statement, and each term must be used with its settled meaning.
